etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bekenen, beknen, becnen, beknien, from Old English bēacnian, bēcnian, bīecnan (“to signal; beckon”), from Proto-West Germanic *bauknōn, *bauknijan (“to signal”), from *baukn (“signal; beacon”). Cognate with Old Saxon bōknian, Old High German bouhnen, Old Norse bákna. More at beacon.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To wave or nod to somebody with the intention to make the person come closer.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: His distant friends, he beckons near.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: It beckons you to go away with it.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To seem attractive and inviting

quote.citation: 2016, “Into the Unknown”, in Brandon Michael Armstrong, Joshua Ross Kaufman, Justin Isaac Rubenstein, Patrick Nolen McHale (lyrics), Over the Garden Wall (Original Television Soundtrack)‎[1], performed by Jack Jones:
quote.text: How the gentle wind / Beckons through the leaves / As autumn colors fall

definitions.definition: A sign made without words; a beck.

quote.citation: c. 1734, Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, A Dissertation on Parties:
2020, Abi Daré, The Girl With The Louding Voice, Sceptre, page 110:
quote.text: He turn to me, make a beckon with the key in his hand.

definitions.definition: A children's game similar to hide and seek in which children who have been "caught" may escape if they see another hider beckon to them.
